items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: So she was playing and then she finally looked over at me and she goes, “You play the intro.”

ctx.x: It is. It was actually pretty cool for Bucky too, which is the funny part. He was so excited. Because I got the call first and I could do literally one day. I flew in from Georgia, did the gig, flew out the next day to a gig in Clarksville, Tennessee and they still had another day. So somewhere before the date they called me and said, “Do you think your father would do the date?” I said, “He’s in the book, I said, “he’ll go anywhere.” So he got there. I was there. I got there at 10 AM. Me and Al Schmidt were the…

lot of fun because you know we did “The Christmas Song” for another record at the same date, “Chestnuts roasting on an open fire” and she was trying to play the intro and she was under the gun ‘cause she was the director. And she’d be like thinking about everything that’s going on. So she was playing and then she finally looked over at me and she goes, “You play the intro.” And I was like okay. And that was like, that’s something we’d talk about, you know, it was Bucky Pizzarelli 101 because every class that I…
That’s not a good feeling if you’re supposed to set up the singer and it comes for their entrance and they can’t —

items.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I mean Diana Krall, we have talked about that too, is that she’s had to change personnel.

ctx.x: You know because too often you go to the clubs even and you pay quite a bit of money to get in and you’re looking at good musicians, but it’s not a band. And sometimes you feel a little bit, well this is personal, sometimes I feel a little bit cheated when I’m looking over and I’m seeing somebody tell chord changes to somebody.

Yeah. Oh I mean I think it’s hard. Harry Allen is one of my dearest friends. He’s a great tenor saxophone player. And he’ll go out and work with Bill Charlap and Kenny Washington and Peter Washington, and I know he lives and dies by his book. He goes around the world and plays with like a drummer and a bass player somewhere in England, and luckily he’s got Charlap and they have a bit of a vibe. But I know he’s got to put out those charts and you know everybody’s got to know what they’re doing. But actually Bill’s…
brains. We just go zip, zip and it works. So I agree with you about groups, to make a long story longer.
